articles.title: MIT researchers folded flat aluminium panels into a room-sized, load-bearing structure without interior columns; lab simulations showed greater stiffness while using roughly two-thirds as much material
articles.summary: We have all tried origami, folding paper into different shapes and sizes.
articles.body: We have all tried origami, folding paper into different shapes and sizes. But what if I told you that engineers at MIT are using a completely different material for their origami? MIT researchers have developed an origami-inspired construction method that can turn flat aluminium sheets into lightweight, rigid structures capable of bearing loads without interior support columns. According to a report published by MIT news on October 27, 2026, the technique uses folded modular components to create complex structural shells and could potentially make construction faster, simpler and more material-efficient.The team demonstrated the approach by assembling a 23-foot sculpture made from folded aluminium pieces, which was suspended in the atrium of the Boston Public Library. According to the researchers, computer simulations indicated that their structures could be about 3.5 times stiffer than those made using certain other structural origami techniques, while requiring only about two-thirds as much material. This combination of strength and reduced material use could make the method worth exploring for projects where conventional construction techniques are difficult, expensive or require heavier structural components.How does the origami-inspired construction method work?The idea behind this method is quite simple. Researchers at MIT are folding flat aluminium panels into carefully designed geometric shapes that can be connected to create larger, rigid structures. Researchers have also developed an automated design tool that helps determine the shapes and configurations required for a particular structure, making it easier to turn a digital design into physical components without having to work out every fold and connection manually.Once the design is ready, computer-controlled machines cut the individual components from flat aluminium sheets, which are then folded and assembled using basic hand tools, such as screwdrivers, without requiring large-scale welding equipment. This means that much of the preparation can happen before the components reach the construction site, where they can be connected to form the intended structure.When connected, these folded components form a network of beams that provides strength and stability to the overall structure. Each component plays a role in supporting the larger framework, allowing the researchers to create more complex shapes without relying on interior support columns. The team is also exploring how this approach can be adapted to different designs, potentially making it easier to build structures of varying shapes and sizes using the same basic construction principle.Why could this method change construction?One of the biggest advantages of this method is that it allows large structures to be made from relatively lightweight components that are easier to transport and assemble. Since the aluminium panels can be cut and prepared in advance and put together using basic hand tools, the process could reduce the need for heavy equipment and specialised construction work at the site. It could also make transportation more convenient, as flat panels can take up less space before they are assembled into their final form.This could be particularly useful in situations where buildings need to be set up quickly, such as after earthquakes, floods or other natural disasters. The researchers believe the method could eventually help create emergency shelters that can be transported as flat panels and assembled when needed, making it easier to provide temporary housing in places where conventional construction may be difficult. Instead of transporting bulky prefabricated structures, teams could potentially carry the individual components and assemble them where they are required.Beyond buildings, the technique could also find applications in aerospace engineering, modular robotics, building facades and sound-dampening panels. Its ability to create rigid structures while using less material could make it useful in projects where reducing weight without compromising structural performance is important. For instance, lightweight components can be particularly valuable in aerospace applications, where the weight of a structure can influence how efficiently a system operates.While the method still needs to be tested further before it can be used in everyday construction, it offers an interesting way to rethink how buildings and other large structures are designed. If researchers can successfully adapt the technique for real-world projects, it could help make construction more flexible and less dependent on heavy materials and equipment, turning a simple idea of folding flat panels into something with much bigger architectural possibilities.

articles.title: Europa observa Marruecos desde el espacio y presencia impotente la expansión de una mancha roja
articles.standfirst: La imagen captada por el satélite Copernicus Sentinel-2 muestra una llamativa franja rojiza en una región árida de Marruecos
articles.summary: La imagen captada por el satélite Copernicus Sentinel-2 muestra una llamativa franja rojiza en una región árida de Marruecos
articles.body: Una enorme mancha roja atraviesa el paisaje árido del sur de Marruecos en una imagen captada desde el espacio por el satélite europeo Copernicus Sentinel-2. La fotografía, publicada por la Agencia Espacial Europea (ESA) el 20 de febrero de 2026, muestra una extensa franja de color escarlata en los alrededores de Uarzazat, una región situada a las puertas del Sáhara. El contraste con los tonos ocres y marrones del terreno ha llamado la atención por su apariencia poco habitual. Sin embargo, no se trata de una catástrofe natural ni de una anomalía que esté tiñendo el suelo de rojo. La imagen corresponde a una composición de falso color que utiliza información del infrarrojo cercano para distinguir la vegetación. La captura se realizó en enero de 2026, durante la estación húmeda, y permite observar cómo las plantas y los cultivos se distribuyen junto a los cauces de agua en un territorio marcado por la aridez. La clave de este fenómeno visual está en la forma en que las plantas reflejan la radiación. La vegetación sana devuelve una gran cantidad de luz infrarroja cercana, invisible para el ojo humano. Al procesar los datos del satélite y representar esa señal mediante el color rojo, las zonas cubiertas de plantas adquieren una tonalidad intensa que destaca sobre el terreno desnudo. Esta técnica permite a los científicos estudiar la distribución y el estado de la vegetación con una precisión que sería difícil de conseguir mediante una fotografía convencional. En la imagen, cuya resolución alcanza los diez metros, se distinguen parcelas agrícolas, áreas vegetadas y pequeños afluentes que recorren la región. Por tanto, el color no refleja el aspecto real del paisaje, sino una forma de hacer visibles datos que normalmente pasarían inadvertidos. La forma ramificada de la mancha también tiene una explicación. Las zonas rojizas siguen principalmente el recorrido de los ríos y sus afluentes, cuyos márgenes concentran buena parte de la vegetación. Durante el invierno y la primavera, estos cursos de agua estacionales pueden transportar cantidades importantes de agua, mientras que en verano muchos de ellos reducen su caudal o llegan a secarse. La fotografía permite identificar, además, la ciudad de Uarzazat, situada al norte de la principal franja roja, y el embalse de El Mansour Eddahbi, que aparece oscuro en esta composición. También se distingue el complejo solar Noor, una enorme instalación de más de 3.000 hectáreas situada a unos diez kilómetros al norte de la ciudad. Sus espejos concentran la radiación solar para generar calor y producir electricidad, incluso después de la puesta de sol gracias a sus sistemas de almacenamiento térmico.

articles.title: China’s secretive space plane spotted docked to another spacecraft in orbit; US military intelligence agency releases rare image revealing a new detail about Beijing’s mysterious space programme
articles.summary: US Defence Intelligence Agency (DIA) has released a rare photograph of China's secretive Shenlong space plane, showing it attached to another spacecraft
articles.body: US Defence Intelligence Agency (DIA) has released a rare photograph of China's secretive Shenlong space plane, showing it attached to another spacecraft in orbit with its cargo compartment open. The image, released on Monday, was taken in May 2024 by a US satellite from about 90 kilometres away. It offers a clearer look at the Chinese spacecraft and its activities in space, about which Beijing has revealed very little.The image was captured when Shenlong was carrying out its third mission. A satellite called WorldView-3, operated by US imagery company Vantor, previously known as Maxar, photographed the vehicleThe picture shows Shenlong's wings and open payload bay, the compartment used to carry equipment into space. Another spacecraft is visible at its rear, with solar panels extended on either side. However, the identity of this satellite and the reason it was connected to Shenlong remain unknown.According to Space.com, the photograph has a resolution of 4.5 centimetres per pixel. Earlier images taken by observers on Earth had shown the Chinese vehicle in orbit, but they offered fewer details. A less detailed version of the same photograph was also presented by the US Space Force in South Korea in 2024. The clearer image has now appeared in the DIA's Challenges to Security in Space report.China's Shenlong space planeChina has been testing Shenlong for six years, but much of its work remains undisclosed. The spacecraft is designed to travel into orbit aboard a rocket and return to Earth by landing on a runway. This makes it reusable, unlike spacecraft that cannot be recovered after completing their missions.Its first flight took place in September 2020 and lasted just two days. The next mission was much longer, with Shenlong spending 276 days in orbit. Its third flight continued for 268 days before ending in September 2024.China launched the vehicle for a fourth time on February 7, 2026. It travelled aboard a Long March-2F rocket from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre. Chinese state news agency Xinhua described the mission as part of efforts to develop reusable spacecraft technology for peaceful purposes.However, the Chinese authorities have not publicly explained what equipment Shenlong carries or the specific experiments being conducted during its flights.According to Aero Time, the spacecraft's appearance has also attracted attention. It has wings, two tail fins and a central payload bay, giving it a design similar to the American X-37B space plane. Both vehicles can spend long periods in orbit before returning to Earth.Objects detected near ShenlongThe photograph is not the only reason Shenlong has attracted attention. During several missions, observers have detected objects moving near the spacecraft, raising questions about the activities taking place in orbit.One such incident occurred in June 2026, during Shenlong's fourth mission. American space intelligence company LeoLabs detected an object near the Chinese vehicle and examined observations collected through its global monitoring network.Following its analysis, the company said it had determined with high confidence that the object had been released by Shenlong. It also noted that similar releases had occurred during earlier missions.An object was also observed during Shenlong's third flight, while its second mission in 2023 involved another release. During that earlier flight, the spacecraft may also have carried out proximity and rendezvous operations.These are manoeuvres in which spacecraft move close to one another in orbit. Such movements can allow vehicles to approach other objects in space, although the purpose of Shenlong's reported activities has not been confirmed.There is also another possible explanation. The spacecraft may have been discarding equipment it no longer needed before returning to Earth. With little information available about the missions, observers have not been able to establish exactly what these objects were or why they were released.The US secretive reusable space planeShenlong has often been compared with the Boeing-built X-37B, a reusable robotic spacecraft operated by the US Space Force. The American vehicle also carries out extended missions in orbit, although many details of its operations are not made public.Some of the experiments conducted aboard the X-37B have been disclosed. During its eighth mission, the US Space Force announced plans to test laser communications between satellites and a quantum inertial sensor. The latter is designed to help spacecraft navigate without depending on GPS.Earlier missions examined aerobraking, a method of changing a spacecraft's orbit, and the effects of space radiation on seeds. Another experiment investigated the possibility of collecting solar energy in space and transmitting power back to Earth.The US has also released relatively few photographs of the X-37B while it is operating in orbit. In February 2025, the Space Force made public an image that appeared to show the vehicle with its payload bay doors open.

articles.title: Meet Isaac Nelson, the 13-year-old Florida boy whose EcoScouts team released over 23,000 native clams, rescued 3,000 mangrove propagules and built oyster gardens estimated to filter 250,000 gallons of water daily
articles.summary: At just 13, Isaac Nelson is tackling an environmental challenge that has troubled Florida's coastal ecosystems for years.
articles.body: At just 13, Isaac Nelson is tackling an environmental challenge that has troubled Florida's coastal ecosystems for years. Armed with scientific curiosity, community support and a determination to restore the waters around Jupiter Inlet, the young conservationist has turned his childhood passion into a hands-on restoration mission. Through EcoScouts, the youth organisation he founded at seven, Nelson is helping revive marine habitats, protect native species and demonstrate how young people can contribute to environmental recovery.Bringing native clams back to jupiter inletAccording to Jupiter Brief, Nelson's latest conservation effort has returned approximately 23,000 juvenile native clams to local waters, offering hope for a species that has become increasingly scarce in the inlet.The project began when Nelson located just 30 surviving clams in nearby estuaries. Working with the Whitney Laboratory for Marine Bioscience at the University of Florida, he helped facilitate their breeding, resulting in thousands of juveniles. The EcoScouts subsequently introduced the young clams into the inlet, using protective mesh bags in selected locations to reduce predation and improve their chances of survival.The Barron Prize highlights the initiative as part of Nelson's wider effort to rebuild the natural systems that support marine biodiversity. Native clams play an important ecological role by filtering water, supporting food webs and helping maintain conditions necessary for seagrass habitats.Oyster gardens that clean the waterNelson's work extends beyond clam restoration. According to Jupiter Brief, EcoScouts has installed 120 vertical oyster gardens using recycled shells collected from local restaurants with support from the West Palm Beach Fishing Club.Volunteers string the shells onto steel wires and suspend them beneath docks, allowing oysters to grow while creating habitats for other marine organisms. The Barron Prize estimates that the developing oyster gardens filter approximately 250,000 gallons of water daily.Beyond improving water quality, these installations provide shelter for marine life and offer residents a practical way to participate in conservation. Community workshops organised with local partners have helped turn the project into a collaborative effort involving families and waterfront property owners.Rebuilding the mangrove shorelineShoreline erosion and heavy boat traffic around the historic Jupiter Lighthouse previously contributed to the removal of native mangroves and living shoreline habitat. According to the Barron Prize, Nelson responded by rescuing more than 3,000 dried-out mangrove propagules and nurturing them in a nursery in his backyard.His work subsequently expanded through a partnership with the Bureau of Land Management, resulting in a permanent mangrove nursery near the lighthouse. The young trees are intended to help restore natural shoreline protection as construction work progresses. Mangroves are vital coastal ecosystems, helping stabilise banks, provide wildlife habitat and buffer shorelines against erosion.Using technology to track recoveryNelson has also developed an underwater benthic camera designed to capture high-resolution footage for up to 48 hours, substantially exceeding the typical 60-minute battery life of comparable equipment, according to the Barron Prize. With AI-enabled species identification, the system can help researchers catalog marine biodiversity and track inlet restoration over time.A young conservationist with bigger goals“The conservation films and scientific programs Nelson has launched have attracted national attention,” Jupiter Brief reported. Yet his work remains rooted in local action, with EcoScouts continuing to seek volunteers and waterfront property owners to expand its projects.His efforts show that environmental responsibility doesn't have to wait until adulthood. By combining research, innovation and community participation, Nelson is helping give Jupiter Inlet a stronger chance at ecological recovery.Images Courtesy: istock and Barron Prize

articles.title: AI has come for Arizona’s water
articles.summary: Arizona has long courted big business, from tech to agriculture. Now the state is facing a water crisis. Are data centers the breaking point?
articles.body: A hulking gray giant rises from the desert. Inside, engineers create the force behind our phones and computers and appliances, our streaming services and search engines and chatbots and vibe-coded apps and websites. The complex is simultaneously massive and squat, dwarfed by the mountains that surround it, and it is endless. I drive past one building, and then another, and then the ground opens up where construction crews have dug up the earth so a third building can rise. There is a parking lot, and then another, and then another. There is an empty lot on the other side of the street, full of cars and the occasional food truck to feed the thousands of laborers who are busy transforming this expanse of desert into an industrial park. There is dust, so much of it, choking the air. I stand before the savior of Arizona’s economy. Like all great deities, it demands sacrifice. In the desert, nothing is more precious than water, and water is what must be given — nearly 5 million gallons a day, every day, sourced from Phoenix’s municipal supply. The offering has been well worth it. All of this is the fruit of the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world’s leading producer of microchips. Its Arizona operation is the result of a pre-pandemic gamble Phoenix made to revive its sluggish economy, which never quite rebounded from the Great Recession. Now TSMC’s foundry looms over the city’s outskirts. TSMC is a success story, one that some local leaders may have hoped to repeat with hyperscale data center developments. The progression may have seemed natural: The Grand Canyon State is not only home to the largest chip factory this side of the Pacific but also 172 data centers, neither of which faced much pushback. But the newer, larger developments being proposed from Phoenix to Tucson demand more of everything — more water, more power, more land — than Arizonans are willing to give. Where TSMC was welcomed with open arms and the first wave of data centers was largely ignored, new developments are facing mass backlash in Arizona, where a grassroots, surprisingly bipartisan coalition of residents has united against data centers. In reporting this story, I spoke to local activists and economic developers, elected officials and their angry constituents. I sat in on city council meetings where people lined up by the dozens to speak up against data center projects, and in cozy suburban homes where tight-knit groups of former strangers told me about the struggle that brought them together. I pored over maps of Arizona’s dry, cracked landscape with laypeople who, over the past two years, have made themselves experts on zoning and land use and water consumption so they can understand the beast they’re trying to fight. The locals on both sides of this debate claim to want the same thing: a better, more prosperous Arizona. Their visions for achieving it, however, are completely at odds. In Arizona and elsewhere, data center developers have tried to win over locals by making enticing promises about the jobs, tax revenue, and infrastructure they’ll bring with them. All they ask for in exchange is water — and, they swear, not nearly as much of it as you’d expect. Some hyperscale data centers, like Google’s facility in The Dalles, Oregon, use about 1.5 million gallons a day, about one-third of what TSMC’s Arizona complex consumes in the same timeframe. Those reassurances, however, aren’t enough to assuage Arizonans, who now have to contend with the fact that the state will soon lose access to nearly 30 percent of the water it receives from the Colorado River. Even now, as people across the country sour on AI and fight against data centers in their communities, TSMC’s Arizona operation hums along without significant opposition. And yet it’s impossible to make sense of why Arizonans are so opposed to new data center development without first understanding why they eagerly welcomed TSMC, even though both industries must contend with the issue that has plagued Arizona since its founding: There isn’t enough water. [Image: An irrigation canal that is part of the Central Arizona Project, which brings water to Phoenix from the Colorado River. For as long as anyone could remember, business in Arizona revolved around the storied “five C’s”: cattle, copper, cotton, citrus, and climate, a catchall for the region’s mild, salubrious winters, which locals say often more than make up for the sweltering summers. Now the state has a sixth C, Arizona native Christine Mackay tells me. “Chips.” The TSMC development is, in a sense, Mackay’s doing. As the head of Phoenix’s economic development office, she spearheaded the effort that brought the Taiwanese giant to the Sonoran Desert. In 2020, while the global economy was all but shut down, TSMC made an announcement. The same forces that brought the world to a standstill had created even more demand for TSMC’s products, and in response, TSMC would be opening an advanced semiconductor foundry — a “fab,” in industry jargon — in Phoenix. Initially, TSMC predicted that it would pour $12 billion into Arizona’s economy by 2029. Since then, TSMC’s projected expenditure in the state has ballooned to $265 billion, what the company touts as the largest foreign direct investment in US history. [Image: The TSMC Arizona headquarters in Phoenix. TSMC just put the finishing touches on its second fab in a formerly desolate swath of north Phoenix, with a third under construction and plans for several more underway. This buildout has been more than a decade in the making. TSMC started shopping around for a US location in 2016. That year, Mackay said, the company put out a request for proposals through a codename. No one won. “We aren’t a group that takes no for an answer,” Mackay said proudly. Her office asked TSMC executives what they thought Arizona was missing, and then spent the next three years addressing their concerns. In 2019, Phoenix sent a delegation to Taiwan to share a new development plan for a science and technology park, the nucleus of which would be a factory, ideally one of TSMC’s fabs. “They agreed they needed to come back and take another look at Phoenix,” Mackay told me. Her team showed them two locations: Laveen, Arizona, a suburb southwest of Phoenix, and, just north of the city, an undeveloped area roughly the size of Manhattan called Biscuit Flats, so named, Mackay told me, because “it’s as round and flat as a biscuit.” “That very day,” she recalled, “they said, ‘This could work.’” What followed was a flurry of development unlike anything the state has ever seen. TSMC has brought more than 3,500 jobs to the state, and an entire economy has sprung up to support the company’s Arizona operation. Much like in Taiwan — where the company accounts for nearly one-tenth of Taiwan’s gross domestic product — TSMC has become, if not the center of the universe, then at least a galaxy unto itself. The company controls an estimated 70 percent of the global chip market, and its contracts with Apple and Nvidia alone make up more than one-third of its annual revenue. (Apple and Nvidia design their own chips, but they don’t produce them. The complex manufacturing process is instead largely outsourced to TSMC.) [Image: This semiconductor manufacturing facility has more than 3,500 employees. TSMC has changed swaths of Phoenix — its landscape, its industries — and it has brought with it jobs and prosperity. Locals fear that the new hyperscale data center developments will do the former but not the latter, consuming resources while contributing little to the community. Mackay, who has worked as an economic developer for over 30 years, didn’t experience significant pushback when she helped court data center developments in the past. “The first 10 data centers I did look like pretty little office buildings,” she said. The new developments being proposed are neither pretty nor little. The durability of these chemicals means they won’t be degraded during the manufacturing process, which can involve hundreds or even thousands of steps. But the qualities that make PFAS so essential to chipmaking are precisely what make them so dangerous to people. Some researchers have linked forever chemicals to liver and kidney issues, high cholesterol, birth defects, and various cancers. Arizona’s historic megadrought was set in motion well before any part of the tech industry gained a foothold in the Grand Canyon State. It’s an almost cartoonishly simple issue of supply and demand, one whose consequences are complex and still uncertain. Hotter and drier summers in the Rocky Mountains are drying up the Colorado River, the source of more than one-third of Arizona’s water. At the same time, Arizona’s aquifers are being drained far faster than they can be replenished. The latter is a problem of demand, the former one of supply. Together, they add up to a crisis over a century in the making. The 1922 Colorado River Compact — the agreement that determines how much of the river’s water to allocate to seven states — simultaneously overestimated the long-term supply of water and underestimated the demand. Legislators in 1922 could not have foreseen the midcentury population boom or the severity of climate change. But this alone does not explain Arizona’s current water woes. There’s also the matter of Arizona’s dwindling aquifers. The culprit there isn’t population growth or heavy industry, at least not in the way most people think of it. It’s agriculture, an extractive, hyperindustrialized process unto itself. Arizona’s now romanticized five C’s were largely brought to the state from elsewhere, and they continue to use far more water than a casual observer imagines or expects. You can’t grow cotton and citrus in the desert, nor can you raise cattle, without water — lots of it. Rural farms rely on groundwater; Arizona’s urban and suburban data centers rely on municipal water, much of it sourced from the Colorado River. And Project Blue’s water allotment adds up to a tiny fraction of the water governed by the Tucson Active Management Area, a state-designated region with specific conservation measures in place, including a provision requiring developers to prove they can guarantee a 100-year supply of water for their projects. The active management area comprised about 326,000 acre-feet in 2024, most of which was slated for residential use. And yet it’s not AI safety, air pollution, or fears of AGI-enabled economic collapse but water that dominates the data center debate in Arizona and elsewhere, even when those other issues are raised, too. More broadly, recent concerns over data centers’ water usage may stem from Empire of AI, a 2025 bestseller by journalist Karen Hao that traces the rise of OpenAI — and, for all its journalistic merits, significantly overestimates one data center’s water usage by a factor of 1,000. Partly in response to Hao’s book, and to the widespread backlash to data center construction, the AI industry has gone on the defensive, but hardly anyone is buying what they’re selling, even when they’re telling the truth. It’s easy to make fun of Sam Altman’s self-exculpatory assertion that it takes more water to grow a single almond than to make 38,000 ChatGPT queries, or to quibble with his lazy math, but the general sentiment is nonetheless true. Globally, agriculture uses about 70 percent of the world’s fresh water; the same is true in Arizona, though agriculture accounted for just 0.4 percent of the state’s gross domestic product in 2023. One could argue that, unlike data centers, farms are necessary for human life — although most of the crops grown around the world are used for biofuels, or to feed livestock, not people. But many locals maintain that any amount of water used for AI is too much. The No Desert Data Center Coalition encourages Arizonans to look beyond the issue of water, tying its fight against Project Blue to a bigger, more fraught battle against extractive industry in all its forms, urging the state and local governments to prioritize industries that revitalize the land instead of further destroying it. Coalition members describe data centers as crucial infrastructure that powers the “cruelty industry,” emphasizing the connections between tech, mass surveillance, and the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. Still, the broader opposition to data centers seemingly always comes back to water. The concern is especially acute in the drought-stricken state, which lost up to one-third of its Colorado River allotment in late August. Tucson, which sources about 70 percent of its water from the Colorado River, has been preparing for this moment for years. Since 2003, the city has used its excess Colorado River water, which flows to the city through a 326-mile network of aqueducts, to recharge the Avra Valley aquifer. Tucson recently expanded its groundwater treatment plant, opening a dedicated facility to cleanse the aquifer of forever chemicals. Through its conservation efforts, Tucson has banked enough groundwater to sustain its residents for an estimated 47 years, but locals say that water should be used for them and their families, not to enrich tech companies in California. The opposition to Project Blue has rallied around a succinct slogan: NOT ONE DROP FOR DATA. Widespread opposition has done little to temper Beale’s ambitions. In the midst of the Project Blue saga, news broke that the developer was looking into building a data center campus in Marana, a rural town 20 miles northwest of Tucson. Beale submitted an application to the Town Council last October, asking it to rezone two adjoining 300-acre plots. One of the properties was owned by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The other belongs to a trust connected to Herb Kai, a member of the Town Council who boasts more than three decades in public service. The Kais are the biggest landowners in town. The patriarch, Cantonese immigrant John Kai, moved to Marana in the 1930s. John, whose descendants remember him as savvy and tenacious, evaded the racist federal ban on Chinese immigrants by assuming a new identity. In Marana, he earned a living hauling vegetables to and from Tucson for the town’s farmers. Eventually he had enough money to buy a plot of his own, where he cultivated cotton. Kai slowly built up his holdings and diversified his investments, and in so doing helped transform once-sleepy Marana into a bustling little town. It is now one of the fastest-growing communities in southern Arizona. Its population has increased by nearly 25 percent since 2020, now hovering around 65,000, but its leaders still think there’s plenty of room to grow. The town is nearly three times the size of Boston and has one-tenth of the population — at least for now. “You’ll talk to people and they’ll say this Town Council has never met a development they didn’t like,” Marana resident Jackie McGuire told me. McGuire, a cybersecurity analyst, moved to Marana from California 15 years ago. She still misses the near-perfect climate of the Bay Area and the easy access to the best Vietnamese food in the country, and her bright pink hair looks out of place in the town, where most people are conservative and many are Mormon. But she loves the desert and the life she has built there. And now the Town Council, she said, is poised to destroy exactly what drew her to Marana in the first place. Though she had never been involved in local politics, McGuire was one of dozens of Marana residents to speak out against Beale’s proposal at a Town Council meeting in December. [Image: Jackie McGuire, described by some as a “liberal with pink hair,” found herself elected to Marana’s Town Council on an anti-data center platform. “I had my children here. I’m raising my children here,” McGuire said. “The town has done a phenomenal job of creating public spaces where people want to come out of their houses and socialize.” The data center, she said, would be an “eyesore,” but her opposition to it isn’t purely aesthetic. McGuire, who worked on Wall Street in the years leading up to the Great Recession, is worried that the AI bubble is about to burst. “One thing I find curious that Beale hasn’t mentioned is that they’re a subsidiary of a company called Blue Owl,” which is currently embroiled in a class action lawsuit for securities fraud, McGuire said. “For what it’s worth,” she added, “I make a living on cloud computing. This AI bubble bursting is going to materially impact my ability to pay my mortgage, and I will have to pivot. I don’t want that for the entire town of Marana.” The Town Council did not heed McGuire’s warnings, nor did they listen to the other people who pleaded that they reject Beale’s proposal. Beale’s promises were enticing: $407 million in tax revenue over the next decade, more than one-third of which would go directly to Marana. A data center, the town’s leaders claimed, would be in Marana’s best interest. The Town Council had in fact passed an ordinance in 2024 restricting data center development. Any facility built in the town would be prohibited from using Marana’s water supply for its cooling systems and would have to adhere to design and noise requirements. Developers would also have to get documentation from the utility provider with proof that there’s sufficient electricity to power a data center. There would be jobs, good ones. Members of various trade unions attended the Town Council meetings and spoke out in support of the data center. Beale employees were present, too, and they brought signs that said “Yes for data centers” to distribute to supporters. No one took them. With the exception of Kai, who recused himself from the proceedings, the council unanimously voted to rezone the land. Marana residents fought back: They collected around 2,800 signatures on petitions asking for a referendum on the data center, only to have the town reject them on a technicality. Residents sued the town, and so did Beale. In the middle of all this, McGuire and three other data center opponents decided to run for Town Council. Their tagline was “Marana for the People.” They held town halls and knocked on hundreds of doors. McGuire, whose politics and presentation are out of step with those of most Marana residents, told me she focused on local policies when talking to voters. “I saw more than one person be like, ‘I can’t believe I’m going to have to vote for a liberal with pink hair just to get rid of this stupid fucking data center,’” McGuire told me. Unlike the other insurgent candidates, she won. [Image: The site of the proposed Luckett Road data center in Marana, Arizona. McGuire, now a member of the Town Council, still worries about the long-term effects a data center will have on her community. Beyond the water and power use, she noted that the chips that power data centers have a shorter shelf life than tech companies’ financials would suggest. In other words, the chips themselves will depreciate more quickly than their financial models take into account. Beale declined to comment on this particular line of criticism, but Burkart emphasized the tax revenue the project will bring to Marana. He also noted the project’s low water footprint. After construction is complete, the Marana facility will use roughly 6.6 million gallons a year. The costs and uncertainties of data center construction are so massive that some major tech companies lack the cash, or the desire, to pay for them outright. McGuire said Beale’s two projects in Arizona would cost a combined $120 billion to build, money that would be funded with private equity and debt, a figure Beale rebuts. According to Burkart, the two projects will cost a combined $8.6 billion. Debt financing isn’t unusual in the tech industry, but the data center buildout requires so much capital that even major financial firms can’t go it alone. Nvidia recently worked with a consortium of six major financial firms that included Blackstone, BlackRock, and Goldman Sachs to finance $500 billion for AI compute; this atypical financing push has been described as more a series of partnerships and memos of understanding than closed deals. For small towns hoping to ride the AI wave, it’s also a risky one. Pulitzer Prize-winning historian Liaquat Ahamed has compared the new AI economy to the railroad boom of the late 19th century, when a handful of companies, armed with generous government contracts, remade the country in their own image and tanked the global economy in the process. The advent of the railroad made Arizona what it is today. It connected the homesteads and ranches scattered throughout the desert to international markets, and to the whims and caprices of global capital. On a blazing Wednesday morning in early August, I stepped out of my air-conditioned car and into the Wild West. There was a miner’s cabin and a sheriff’s office and an abandoned farmhouse, a church, and a saloon where, I understood, gunfights had broken out in the past and would someday break out again. There was a small, inoperable well, an opera house and a carpenter’s studio, a dressmaker, a blacksmith, a bank. There was a ranch complex and an “Oriental Cafe” right next door to the undertaker. Here was a small civilization, an oasis in the inhospitable desert, surrounded on all sides by mountains. Not quite a ghost town, but nonetheless devoid of people. When I walked into the lobby of the Pioneer Living History Museum in north Phoenix, the woman behind the counter asked if I was sure I wanted to be there. Aside from the telephone museum — which I wouldn’t be able to peruse anyway, since the feral peacock that lives on the property had gotten in again, and he was in a foul mood — the whole thing was outside. Outside that day was 105 degrees. The volunteer actors who typically populate the little town weren’t there. Too hot. A paved sidewalk that certainly didn’t exist in the pioneer days led me to the door of a well-appointed Victorian home built in the 1890s for a J. Marion Sears and his family. Though the paint’s yellow exterior now cracks under the intense Arizona sun, it was clear the Searses had lived well. The Sears home, a placard boasted, was one of the first wood-framed homes to be erected in the city. Lumber was hard to come by before the railroad’s tracks reached Phoenix in 1887. Before then all goods had to be freighted into the city, typically by teams of mules, and in fact that was how Sears had made a small fortune. A Confederate veteran, he arrived in the Arizona Territory in 1878 and made a living as a freighter and cattle rancher. Though they lived in the desert, the Sears family homestead was fruitful: Tidy orchards provided them with apples, pears, apricots, figs, and almonds. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: This bounty was not unusual, but, as detailed in Thomas E. Sheridan’s Arizona: A History, it was precarious. The Sears family, like other white settlers, tended to their crops with water sourced from an intricate network of canals, the first of which was built by the Swilling Irrigation and Canal Company in 1867. Its owner, Jack Swilling, was a hardworking, hard-drinking entrepreneur who often supplemented his whiskey with liquid morphine. He was not, however, a particularly talented engineer, a limitation that ultimately didn’t matter much, because Swilling neither designed nor built the canals that helped white men settle the Salt River Valley. That work had been done centuries ago by the Hohokam, a pre-Columbian people who tapped into the Salt and Gila rivers to build a thriving agricultural civilization in the middle of the desert. By the 16th century the Hohokam had fallen. Their descendants scattered; their canals sat idle and eventually went dry until Swilling thought to revive them. Swilling’s innovation kicked off a new wave of development in Arizona. Homesteaders flocked to the territory, as did speculators who were less interested in eking a living out of the land than getting rich off what lay beneath it. The earth didn’t yield much in the way of precious metals, but it was rich in copper, and it wasn’t long until investors from San Francisco and New York opened up mines and smelters. Across the territory, family farms were crowded out by capital. The cattle conglomerates came first, and with them came alfalfa. Agricultural conglomerates planted wheat and barley and, after some botanical experimentation, tens of thousands of citrus trees, until it all dried up in the national depression of 1893, two years into a drought that drained the canals and the rivers that fed them. After a few parched years Arizona was bailed out by the federal government, which built a reservoir so the people of the Salt River Valley would never again experience privation. Theodore Roosevelt christened his namesake dam in 1911 and predicted that, having harnessed the power of water, the valley would someday be “one of the richest agricultural areas in the world.” Well before it became a state, overconsumption of water was encoded into Arizona’s DNA. Propped up by feats of engineering, Arizona’s economy steadily plugged along until the first World War, when the industrial demands of militarization transformed the desert state into an economic powerhouse. Suddenly there was insatiable demand for everything Arizona produced: citrus and cattle to feed the troops, alfalfa to feed the cattle, cotton for airplane tires, copper for manufacturing. Fortunes grew. “Alfalfa was King,” the Arizona Republican declared in 1917, “Cotton was Queen, and every Dairy Cow was a Princess.” When the war ended and the Depression tanked the economy a decade later, it all went bust again. It took another war to revive the economy. The first indication that things were turning around came in 1939, when a new war in Europe sent metal prices soaring. Even before the United States entered World War II in 1941, the federal government had started looking to Arizona as a training ground for the military, building out flight schools and Air Force bases in the desert. Arizona’s industrial economy is the product of two world wars — and TSMC’s investment in the state is part of a trade war with China, a 21st-century arms race where the end goal is not a nuclear bomb but something critics say is akin to it. Looked at this way, Arizona’s AI boom isn’t something new; rather, it is more of the same, albeit on a grander scale. “It’s crazy to think about where we used to be and what we used to do,” Mackay, Phoenix’s former economic developer, told me. “You’d disappear out into the desert. I could ride my horse to Indian Bend in Pima all the way to the Verde River without seeing a building.” That route now passes three golf courses, a hospital, an indoor water park, an aquarium, and countless subdivisions and strip malls. The Salt River Valley had a population of 11,000 in 1890. Fifty years and several irrigation projects later, just over 65,000 people lived in Phoenix. Last year, the metropolitan area reported a population of more than 5 million. Shockingly, this development isn’t to blame for Arizona’s perilous lack of water. Population growth hasn’t led to an increase in Arizona’s water consumption. Not only does the average Arizonan consume less water today than in the 1980s, but the state’s overall water use has also dropped by 16 percent since then, a decline almost entirely attributable to reduced agricultural demand. But resource conservation can only go so far when the rivers and aquifers that sustain life in the state are drying up, and locals are understandably furious that they’re being asked to reduce their own water consumption while local officials welcome new water-intensive industries. The land immediately surrounding the Pioneer Living History Museum remains largely undeveloped. Here the past remains unchanged and lovingly maintained in honor of the rugged pioneers who made the desert bloom. This is Arizona’s history. And just five miles south, where TSMC’s engineers manufacture the chips that enable the AI industry to reshape life as we know it, lies Arizona’s future.

articles.title: Wildlife traffickers may have killed her family to capture her; rescued baby gorilla Bili begins a second life in Congo
articles.summary: When Bili the baby gorilla was rescued from wildlife traffickers in Nigeria in 2023, she was sick, frightened, and so young that she needed constant
articles.body: When Bili the baby gorilla was rescued from wildlife traffickers in Nigeria in 2023, she was sick, frightened, and so young that she needed constant reassurance from her human caregivers. For the next three years, she would sleep clinging to a rescuer, gradually recover from illness and learn to trust again. Now, after an international operation moved her to a forest sanctuary in the Republic of the Congo, the young western lowland gorilla is beginning another chapter, with conservationists hoping she may eventually return to the wild.According to CNN's October 16 report, experts believe that some, if not all, of Bili's family members were probably killed when she was taken from her natural habitat for the exotic pet trade. Her precise birthplace remains unknown, with Cameroon, Gabon and the Republic of the Congo among the possible origins. What is known is that she was intercepted in Lagos, Nigeria, in August 2023, when customs officials uncovered an attempted sale of the infant gorilla.Her rescue has since become a story of survival, international cooperation and the challenges of rehabilitating animals traumatised by wildlife trafficking.Rescued from traffickers as an infantBili was only a few months old when Nigeria Customs Service officers seized her following an undercover operation conducted with Focused Conservation, a nonprofit organisation that works to disrupt wildlife trafficking networks. Investigators posed as potential buyers during the operation. Two men were subsequently arrested and convicted in connection with conspiracy, unlawful possession and the attempted sale of a gorilla, CNN reported.The infant was transferred to Drill Ranch, a primate rehabilitation centre in Calabar, Cross River State, operated by the Pandrillus Foundation. There, caregivers discovered that she was unwell and suffering from a fungal infection. Primatologist Lindsay Maess, who cared for Bili at the centre, described her survival as remarkable. Trafficked infant gorillas are particularly vulnerable because they lose the protection and nutrition provided by their mothers and must adapt to unfamiliar surroundings while recovering from illness and trauma.According to CNN, Maess estimated that more than 80% of trafficked gorillas do not survive. Bili's distress was evident in her behaviour. She screamed when she saw a box or cage, while Pandrillus co-founder Peter Jenkins recalled that she clung to his body while sleeping during her first three months in care.“She was very young and needed that security — being loved,” Jenkins told CNN. Bili eventually shared an enclosure with Brendan and Mili, two chimpanzees who had also been rescued from traffickers. Their companionship helped her become more confident and emerge from her shell, Maess said.But recovery at a rescue centre was never intended to be the end of her journey. Bili needed a long-term home where she could continue developing the social and behavioural skills required for a life closer to the wild.A journey across borders to a new homeOn September 21, 2026, Bili began the journey from Calabar to Lagos by road. The trip took approximately 22 hours and was complicated by a vehicle breakdown and other delays. She then travelled on a DHL cargo flight from Lagos to Pointe-Noire, via Libreville, Gabon, arriving in the Republic of the Congo on September 23. From there, she was transported to the Tchimpounga Nature Reserve, a rehabilitation centre operated by the Jane Goodall Institute.The Jane Goodall Institute confirmed the transfer in a September 29 announcement, describing it as a collaborative operation involving conservation organisations, government agencies, customs authorities and transport partners. Bili travelled with Imelda Effiong, the caregiver who had looked after her for three years, and veterinarian Rebeca Atencia, executive director of the Jane Goodall Institute's Republic of the Congo programme.The familiar faces were important during a journey that involved confinement, road travel, air transport and unfamiliar surroundings. At Tchimpounga, Bili has access to indoor and outdoor enclosures featuring forest and savannah environments. Atencia told CNN that the gorilla had adapted well to her new surroundings and demonstrated considerable resilience. The transfer marks a major milestone, but it does not mean Bili can immediately be released into the forest.Can Bili return to the wild?According to CNN, Bili was expected to undergo a 40-day quarantine and health checks before being introduced to Mozambique, a younger female gorilla already living at the sanctuary. The introduction is intended to help her develop social relationships and behaviours that are important for her long-term rehabilitation. If the process goes well, the two gorillas could eventually move to the Lesio-Louna Reserve, a protected area covering approximately 173,000 hectares in the Republic of the Congo. The reserve is managed by the country's Ministry of Forest Economy and the Aspinall Foundation, which runs a gorilla rehabilitation and reintroduction programme.The ultimate goal is to give Bili an opportunity to progress towards living in the wild, although her future will depend on her health, behaviour and ability to adapt. “The hope is that, in time, this group will have the opportunity to progress through the rehabilitation and reintroduction process and ultimately return to a life in the wild,” Atencia told CNN.The wider cost of wildlife traffickingBili's journey also highlights the burden placed on rescue centres after trafficked animals are seized. While arrests and confiscations disrupt illegal trade, sanctuaries must fund years of specialised care, veterinary treatment and rehabilitation. CNN reported that Pandrillus cares for nearly 700 animals and that rescue centres in Nigeria are operating at capacity. Caring for an infant gorilla over several years can cost thousands of dollars in milk alone, apart from veterinary treatment, staff and facilities.Interpol estimates that wildlife crime generates approximately $20 billion annually, according to CNN's report. The trade threatens endangered species while leaving rescued animals with physical and psychological damage that can take years to address.For Bili, the move to Congo offers something she lost when she was taken from the wild: the possibility of growing up in an environment where she can develop relationships with other gorillas and eventually live more independently.Her return to the forest is not guaranteed. But after three years of rehabilitation, an exhausting cross-border journey and a difficult start to life, Bili has been given another opportunity to thrive. As Atencia told CNN, the hope is that rescued gorillas such as Bili will receive “a second chance at a normal life.”

articles.title: Michael Dell says Trump Account 'moment has become a movement'; shares donations from Silicon Valley and beyond; names include SpaceX COO
articles.summary: Michael Dell has hailed the Trump Accounts program as a growing national movement.
articles.body: Michael Dell has hailed the Trump Accounts program as a growing national movement. Dell CEO took to social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) to share the details of fresh contributions from Silicon Valley and beyond. In a reaction pots, Dell wrote, “This is how a moment becomes a movement.” For those unaware, this initiative is designed to give every American child under 18 a stake in the stock market. It has already opened 9 million accounts and is on track to auto-create accounts for all 70 million children using Social Security data.Contributions made by SpaceX COO, Ray Dalio and othersDell's post highlighted a growing list of high-profile donors stepping up to fund Trump Accounts, the tax-deferred investment savings program for American children under 18. Among the names: Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner, who is contributing $250 each to Trump Accounts for more than 140,000 children in Indiana, and hedge fund manager Ray Dalio and his wife Barbara, who are extending similar $250 contributions to children across Connecticut.The biggest single commitment by dollar value came from SpaceX President and COO Gwynne Shotwell, who — along with her husband, Robert — is donating one share of SpaceX stock to each of more than 2 million children, a gift Dell's post pegs at roughly $325 million. The donation is specifically targeted at children between the ages of 11 and 17 in lower-income communities, continuing a pattern Shotwell set earlier this year when she first announced the gift shortly after SpaceX's record-breaking public listing.Dell used the post to personally thank Gerstner for organizing the broader donor push through Invest America, crediting him for turning the concept into reality, and thanked every donor who has stepped up to participate.Read Michael Dell’s complete post hereThis is how a moment becomes a movement. 🚀🇺🇸In Indiana, @altcap’s Brad Gerstner is contributing $250 to Trump Accounts for more than 140,000 young Hoosiers. 🙏@Gwynne_Shotwell and her husband Robert are giving one share of their@SpaceX stock to each of more than 2 million kids, an announced gift valued at roughly $325 million, focused on children ages 11–17 in lower-income communities. 🚀@RayDalio and Barbara Dalio are supporting children across Connecticut with additional $250 contributions. 👏And many more are stepping up.Thank you Brad for organizing @InvestAmerica24and relentlessly turning an idea into reality, and thank you to every donor joining in.Millions of kids starting life as owners. Learning investing. Seeing compounding firsthand. Participating in America’s future.If you have children under 18, claim their accounts now and watch as additional contributions are made.Every child an investor. Every child an owner. Every child with a stake in America's future. 🇺🇸🚀Trump Accounts launched on July 4Trump Accounts launched on July 4, offering a one-time $1,000 contribution from the US Treasury for every child born between 2025 and 2028, with the accounts open more broadly to all American children under 18. According to Gerstner, who has been central to building out the program's donor infrastructure, roughly 9 million accounts are currently open, with plans in motion to automatically create accounts for all 70 million children under 18 nationwide using Social Security data within the coming month.Michael and Susan Dell have themselves been among the largest backers of the initiative, having pledged a combined $6.25 billion earlier this year to fund $250 contributions for children in lower- and middle-income ZIP codes. Beyond individual philanthropy, Gerstner noted that employers are increasingly layering their own contributions on top of the government's, treating it as an extension of existing 401(k)-style benefits.You use AI every day. articles.title: Cardiff Parkway £30m pledge is an insult, Welsh minister says
articles.summary: Wales' transport minister says the cash is a "tiny fraction" of what is needed for Cardiff Parkway.
articles.body:
A £30m rail funding pledge announced by Chancellor John Healey in the Budget is "an insult to the people of Wales", a Welsh government minister says.

Wales' Transport Minister Mark Hooper said the investment in the proposed Cardiff Parkway station was "a tiny fraction" of the cash needed to improve Welsh rail.

The Plaid Cymru-led Welsh government had called on Healey to bring forward £1bn of the £14bn the UK Labour government had promised for long-term rail funding in Wales.

UK government finance minister Emma Reynolds said the cash was part of a £445m package aimed at tackling years of "chronic under-investment" in rail.

Hooper made the comments after a meeting with the UK government in Whitehall on Thursday.

The proposed Cardiff Parkway in the city's eastern St Mellons area would link passengers on the South Wales Metro network to north Wales, Bristol, Manchester and London.

Wales to make £100 energy payments but Plaid ministers say Budget leaves them with cuts

New railway stations part of £14bn UK government funding promise

On Wednesday the chancellor's Budget announcement confirmed cash for three projects in Wales - £2.5m for a science park in Ynys Mon, £11m for a bridge in Port Talbot and £30m for Cardiff Parkway.

UK ministers said that rail funding was part of a £445m package that had been announced at the last Spending Review.

The UK government has already backed plans for five new stations in Cardiff, Newport and Monmouthshire, as well as upgrades in north Wales.

The UK government had previously claimed Cardiff Parkway - whose private developers had plans for the station approved in January 2025 after years of delays - could serve 800,000 passengers every year and support around 6,000 jobs.

Budget documents released on Wednesday said the £30m would "progress delivery" for the scheme.

UK government finance minister Reynolds told Radio Wales Breakfast on Thursday that the £445m to progress rail projects in Wales was because of "chronic underinvestment in Wales" during past Conservative and Tory-Liberal Democrat UK governments.

"We need to clear away the red tape and get the planning in place," she said.

"So the reason that we have given £30m to Cardiff Parkway Rail Station yesterday is because we've done the work together to get the planning in place, so we can get that money flowing."

She said she was "all ready to work" with the Welsh government and Transport for Wales to progress with the project.

Hooper met UK government ministers and officials in Whitehall later on Wednesday to discuss his plans for rail.

He told BBC Wales the £30m announced was a "tiny fraction" of what was needed, saying: "This figure is an insult to the people of Wales."

"The UK government's continued failure to invest in their network in Wales demonstrates, now, more than ever, the need for devolution of rail," he said.

"It's wrong to say these stations aren't shovel-ready. The UK government promised this money in February and since then we've agreed with Network Rail that Transport for Wales will deliver the stations.

"Transport for Wales are ready to start work we just need the UK government to keep their promise. I made this point to the rail minister when I met him today."

The Welsh government said that despite making up 10% of the rail network across Great Britain, just 1% of Network Rail's spending goes to Wales.

Developers had hoped Cardiff Parkway would be operational by 2024, but the planning process was dogged by delays.

Plans were approved by Cardiff council in April 2022, but the broader national interest in the project led the Welsh government under Labour to review the application, before former First Minister Eluned Morgan granted planning permission in January 2025.

articles.title: The asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago may have also set the stage for ants to conquer the planet, with scientists finding a surprising boost from so-called jumping genes hidden in ant DNA
articles.summary: The big dinosaurs ruled Earth for millions of years, only for the tiny ants to take over.
articles.body: The big dinosaurs ruled Earth for millions of years, only for the tiny ants to take over. Around 66 million years ago, an asteroid wiped out the dinosaurs from the face of the Earth forever. But this mass extinction set the stage for other animals to evolve and spread. And ants were among the animals that used that opportunity to the fullest.Today, ants are one of the largest groups of social insects, with more than 15,000 species found around the world. There’s hardly any corner of the Earth where, if you drop a cube of sugar, ants will not attack it. Now, scientists have discovered a genetic factor called “jumping genes” that might be responsible for their rise.New research published in Science Advances suggests that their extraordinary evolutionary success was partly driven by mobile segments of DNA known as transposable elements. This international study, led by Dr. Lukas Schrader of the Institute for Evolution and Biodiversity (IEB) at the University of Münster, Germany, points to a possible genetic link between the environmental upheaval following the asteroid impact and the subsequent expansion of major ant groups.How "Jumping Genes" Helped Ants EvolveJumping genes, as the name suggests, are not genes jumping in your DNA; rather, they are transposable genetic elements. Jumping genes are pieces of DNA that can move to different locations within a genome and produce additional copies of themselves. Scientists once viewed them primarily as “genomic parasites” because, much like viruses, they can multiply without providing any clear benefit to their host. In some cases, their activity can even contribute to disease.Recently, scientists have found that these mobile genetic elements can also create opportunities for mutation and help in the diversification of ants. When scientists compared different groups of ants, they found that the groups with the highest numbers of jumping genes also tended to have more species today. The timing of the gene activity was particularly surprising. They observed that several major ant lineages experienced separate surges in jumping gene activity during the early Paleogene period, about 66 million years ago.As Lukas Schrader explained, “The asteroid impact had dramatic consequences for the environment. We have now found the genomic mechanism that connects these ecological upheavals to the subsequent rapid diversification of the ants: transposable elements.”The evolutionary pattern was not limited to ants; studies have also shown periods of increased jumping gene activity associated with the emergence of new species in other groups, including primates and bats.Boost to Ant CommunicationThese genetic elements have not only helped ants survive but may also have boosted their sense of smell, allowing them to communicate more efficiently through chemical signals.The olfactory receptors that enable ants to detect and respond to smells have been affected by these genetic elements. These receptors are essential to ants' survival and social behaviour. Ants depend heavily on chemical signals to find their way through the environment, identify members of their own colonies, and coordinate activities with other ants.These findings suggest that jumping genes may have helped ants develop their sensory systems, allowing them to adapt to major environmental changes, including those following the extinction of the dinosaurs. More than survival, these changes may also have helped improve their social behaviour. Like bees, ants are highly social insects, and their sensory systems help them detect and interpret the chemical messages that make their complex societies possible.100 Million Years of Ant EvolutionAs ants and dinosaurs coexisted, their evolutionary histories overlapped for millions of years. For the study, the international team compared the genomes of 163 ant species, representing 12 of the 16 ant subfamilies that survive today. Using these genetic comparisons, the researchers reconstructed changes in transposable element activity over approximately 100 million years.As reported by ScienceDaily, these results reveal a striking connection between ancient bursts of jumping gene activity and the later diversification of ants, suggesting that these genetic elements may have contributed to their evolutionary success.The dinosaurs may have lost the planet, but the tiny ants that survived the changing world may have gained a genetic advantage. Scientists now suggest that DNA sequences once dismissed as genomic parasites could have helped ants develop better smell-based communication and diversify into thousands of species. In a strange twist of evolution, the same genetic elements that copy and move themselves around DNA may have helped shape some of the most successful societies in the animal kingdom.

articles.title: This open-source project lets you sync Withings data to other apps without a subscription
articles.summary: An open-source project called YourOwnWeigh lets you reroute where Withings smart scales send your data so you can sync it to other apps.
articles.body: When it was revealed earlier this month that Withings would require new users to subscribe to a Withings Plus subscription to sync heath data from the company’s devices to third-party apps, Tom Anthony, who was already fed up with the Withings mobile app which they describe as a “bloated mess,” became motivated to “free” their scales. Anthony’s solution was to create an open-source project called YourOwnWeigh that reroutes your data away from Withings’ servers so it can be wirelessly synced to other apps and platforms for free. You can read more about the project on GitHub, where you’ll also find quick-start guides on how to get YourOwnWeigh set up, but it mostly consists of a web app running on a server of your choice. If you don’t already operate your own, Anthony says YourOwnWeigh can run entirely on a free CloudFlare account given how little data it’s moving around. The YourOwnWeigh web app handles several tasks, including using Bluetooth to update Withings scales with alternate firmware so they upload data to a non-Withings server you’ve configured. Instead of hosting a copy of Withings’ firmware, it’s downloaded and patched as needed. The web app also imports the scale’s current settings and existing user profiles, and downloads the health data generated by regular weigh-ins. To get that data into Apple Health, Anthony used Apple Shortcuts to create a scheduled automation that pulls the Withings data off the alternate server and imports it into the app, but they’re hoping the community can come up with ways to expand the compatibility to other apps, including Google Health. YourOwnWeigh is also currently limited to just two older models of Withings’ scales. But assuming the firmware on newer models can be patched in a similar manner, expanding the project’s compatibility should be possible.

articles.title: In 1987, an amateur fossil hunter found a T. rex in South Dakota; the $31.8 million skeleton now stands in Abu Dhabi
articles.summary: As children watching dinosaur movies, we all became fascinated by the huge and mysterious creature.
articles.body: As children watching dinosaur movies, we all became fascinated by the huge and mysterious creature. This fascination led the young and amateur fossil hunter Stan Sacrison to uncover one of the most well-preserved specimens of T.Rex ever found.Imagine walking across a field looking for fossils and stumbling upon the bones of one of the most fearsome creatures to have ever walked the Earth. That is more or less what happened to Stan Sacrison in 1987, when he came across bones that would eventually be identified as belonging to a Tyrannosaurus rex, a dinosaur that lived around 67 million years ago.The skeleton was later named Stan after its discoverer and went on to become one of the most famous T. rex specimens in the world, selling for $31.8 million at an auction in 2020 before finding a new home at the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi.How was the T. rex skeleton discovered?The discovery took place in South Dakota's Hell Creek Formation, a geological area known for its rich deposits of fossils from the Late Cretaceous period. Sacrison was looking for fossils when he spotted dinosaur bones weathering out of the ground, including what appeared to be part of a dinosaur's hip. However, the remains were initially misidentified as belonging to a Triceratops, and it was not until 1992, when experts from the Black Hills Institute of Geological Research returned to examine the site, that the bones were correctly identified as those of a T. rex.What followed was a painstaking excavation, with each bone carefully removed from the surrounding rock, cleaned, preserved and recorded before the skeleton could be assembled. The process involved more than 30,000 hours of manual work, eventually bringing together 188 original bones into a remarkably well-preserved specimen. Stan is about 11.7 metres long and is considered one of the more complete T. rex skeletons ever discovered, with its skull being particularly important to researchers studying the anatomy of the dinosaur.Why did Stan sell for $31.8 million?For decades, Stan was kept at the Black Hills Institute in South Dakota, where researchers could study the fossil and visitors could see the enormous predator up close. Its skeleton was also replicated for display in museums around the world, making Stan a familiar sight to dinosaur enthusiasts even before the original specimen went up for sale.In October 2020, the original skeleton was auctioned by Christie's in New York and sold for $31.8 million, far exceeding its pre-sale estimate of $6 million to $8 million. The identity of the buyer was not immediately revealed, and the sale raised concerns among palaeontologists, who worried that such an important fossil might disappear into a private collection and become inaccessible to researchers. The price was a record for a dinosaur fossil at the time, although another dinosaur skeleton, a T. rex named Gus, surpassed it in 2026 after selling for approximately $50.1 million.Where can visitors see Stan today?The mystery surrounding Stan's new owner was partly resolved in March 2022, when Abu Dhabi announced that the skeleton would become a major attraction at its upcoming Natural History Museum. The announcement also revealed that the fossil had been purchased for the museum, bringing an end to speculation about whether the specimen would remain available for public viewing and scientific study.The Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi opened in November 2025, giving Stan a permanent home in the Saadiyat Cultural District. Rather than simply placing the dinosaur in a traditional standing pose, the museum displays Stan in a dramatic scene involving another T. rex, with the two skeletons appearing to clash over a fallen Triceratops. The display draws attention to the fossil's own injuries and bite marks, including evidence of a T. rex bite on Stan's neck, offering visitors a glimpse of the violent encounters that may have taken place during the dinosaur's lifetime.From the moment Sacrison spotted those bones in South Dakota to its record-breaking auction and eventual arrival in Abu Dhabi, Stan has travelled a remarkable distance through both time and geography. The skeleton is a reminder that fossils are not merely remnants of an ancient world; when carefully excavated and made accessible, they can help scientists understand how these animals lived, moved and survived millions of years before humans appeared.

articles.title: Taking antibiotics? Eating a lot of sugar at the same time may make the damage to your gut worse, scientists have found, suggesting that what you eat during a course of antibiotics could affect how well your body recovers
articles.summary: Craving while being unwell is real: the distaste of medicine, bitter pills and syrups. At that moment, we just want to eat something good.
articles.body: Craving while being unwell is real: the distaste of medicine, bitter pills and syrups. At that moment, we just want to eat something good. While the disease is already making us suffer, the restrictions on our diet make recovery almost not worth it anymore. And we end up eating all the junk and sweets that we normally avoid. But do you know that a sugar-rich diet might just be worsening your gut health?According to a new study, eating more sugar while taking antibiotics may intensify the disruption those drugs cause to beneficial gut bacteria. There's a vast ecosystem of bacteria in our gut that evolved with us and helps us digest food, support immune function and perform other essential processes. And the antibiotics that we commonly take cannot always distinguish between harmful bacteria and the enormous community of beneficial microorganisms in our intestines. In some cases, the disruption allows other germs to gain an advantage.How Sugar May Make Antibiotics Harder on Your GutThe study, published in the journal Nature, examined how sugar consumption was associated with changes in the gut microbiome during antibiotic treatment. Researchers found that among patients receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics, higher sugar intake was associated with lower gut bacterial diversity.Researchers from NYU Langone Health, City of Hope and Memorial Sloan Kettering closely monitored 9,419 meals consumed by 173 hospitalised cancer patients and tracked changes in their gut microbiomes. They also analysed stool samples from a subset of these patients.For every additional 100 grams of sweets consumed in the preceding 48 hours, the researchers' model predicted an additional 24.1% decrease in mean gut microbiome alpha diversity in the context of broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure. Alpha diversity is a measure of the variety and distribution of microorganisms within a sample, not a type of bacteria.The more diverse the gut microbiome is, the better it may help maintain a balance between different bacterial populations. The researchers investigated Enterococcus, a group of bacteria that includes species capable of causing serious infections, particularly in vulnerable patients. When antibiotics disturb the gut microbiome, some bacteria can gain an advantage over others. The researchers wanted to understand whether sugar could further influence this process.Experiments with laboratory mice supported this possibility. Mice given sucrose alongside antibiotics experienced a substantially greater increase in enterococcal levels than those receiving antibiotics without the added sucrose. These findings suggest that sugar may influence how certain bacteria respond when antibiotics have already disrupted the gut's microbial balance.However, this does not mean that sugar cancels out the effects of antibiotics or that eating sweets during treatment will automatically lead to an infection. Rather, the study showed how sugar intake was associated with changes in the gut microbiome during antibiotic exposure.What Happens to Gut Bacteria During Antibiotic TreatmentAntibiotics are among the most commonly used medicines for treating bacterial infections, but their effects go beyond the harmful bacteria responsible for the disease. Depending on the antibiotic, they can also affect beneficial microorganisms living in the intestine. When antibiotics reduce these bacterial populations, they can leave behind an environment in which certain microbes find it easier to multiply.One group that scientists are particularly interested in is Enterococcus. While these bacteria can live in the gut without causing problems, certain species can also trigger serious infections, especially in people with weakened immune systems.The new study suggests that sugar intake could influence this process, potentially giving certain bacteria an additional advantage during antibiotic treatment. However, there is an important caveat: the human participants were undergoing blood stem-cell transplantation and were particularly vulnerable to infections. Whether the same pattern occurs in otherwise healthy people taking antibiotics for common infections remains to be investigated.Can Your Diet Help the Gut Recover After Antibiotics?From the research, one thing is clear: diet may play a role in how our gut microbiome responds to antibiotics. To maintain gut health, many people try probiotics to support their gut. That could be helpful in some circumstances, but this study did not establish whether probiotics could prevent the changes observed in patients. Cutting back on sugar-rich foods during an antibiotic course could be worth investigating as a simpler approach, but more research is needed before scientists can establish whether reducing sugar intake leads to better outcomes for people taking antibiotics.The study combined observations from human patients with experiments in mice. While the mouse experiments helped researchers investigate a possible link between sugar and bacterial growth, animal findings do not automatically translate to humans. Further studies involving broader patient populations will be needed to understand how widely these results apply.For now, the research highlights the importance of examining diet alongside antibiotic use. It does not establish that everyone should avoid sugar completely, or that sugar will make the treatment ineffective. Instead, it gives us a reminder that how the body responds to antibiotics may depend not entirely on the medicines alone, but also on what we eat. When doctors tell us to avoid something during a course of medication, instead of taking it as a challenge, we should consider the reasons behind the advice and the research around it. Ultimately, the food we eat contains compounds that may interact with the biological processes affected by our medicines.
