articles.title: Data centers could send US climate pollution skyrocketing
articles.summary: Gas plants built for data centers are poised to undo more than a decade of climate action.
articles.body: The US power sector could release 42 percent more planet-heating carbon dioxide pollution by 2030 than it did in 2025 as it builds out more fossil fuel infrastructure to meet data center electricity demand, according to a new analysis by the Sierra Club. That would essentially wipe out 15 years of greenhouse gas reductions. CO2 emissions from electricity generation would increase by 618 million tons by the end of the decade if planned AI projects are constructed. That’s roughly equivalent to carbon pollution from the electricity use of 128,788,523 homes in a year. The Sierra Club’s estimate is higher than some previous projections from other groups. Another study published by academic researchers in June forecast that electricity demand from data centers and crypto mines could push up power sector emissions by 28 percent by 2030 when compared to a scenario with no data center growth. The outcome depends on how many planned data center projects actually come to fruition, as well as on what type of technology is used to power those facilities. Net US greenhouse gas emission have fallen from a peak of about 6.58 billion metric tons in 2007 to about 5.35 billion metric tons in 2025. But that pollution started ticking back up last year as data centers drove up electricity demand. The Trump administration is incentivising the buildout of fossil fuel infrastructure for data centers while simultaneously rolling back pollution regulations and stalling renewable energy projects. The US is now planning to build more fossil fuel capacity than it has in a decade, according to a separate report published this month by the Environmental Defense Fund.

articles.title: In 2018, Antipodes Island was declared free of invasive mice; eight years later, scientists reported ground beetle numbers 40 times higher, with rove beetles up more than 20-fold after predator removal
articles.summary: When conservation teams confirmed in 2018 that invasive house mice had been removed from Antipodes Island, it marked the end of one of New Zealand’s most
articles.body: When conservation teams confirmed in 2018 that invasive house mice had been removed from Antipodes Island, it marked the end of one of New Zealand’s most ambitious island restoration efforts. The remote subantarctic island had carried mice for more than a century, and their appetite for insects, seeds, plants and occasionally bird eggs had quietly reshaped the ecosystem. Eight years on, scientists have reported that ground beetle numbers are now about 40 times higher than before the mice were removed, while rove beetles have increased more than twentyfold. The findings, published in Conservation Science and Practice, offer a rare long-term measure of what happens when a relentless predator disappears from a small island ecosystem. They also show that ecological recovery is not always immediate, tidy or predictable, but it can be remarkably powerful when the pressure is finally lifted. Read more details about it here:A remote island under pressureAntipodes Island lies in New Zealand’s subantarctic region, a wild and windswept place valued for its seabird colonies, endemic land birds and distinctive invertebrate life. The main island is home to species found nowhere else, including the Antipodes Island snipe, Antipodes parakeet and Reischek’s parakeet. For decades, however, house mice were part of the island’s ecological reality. They arrived through human activity and became established despite the island’s isolation and harsh climate.Their impact was not subtle. Research before the eradication found that mice preyed heavily on surface-dwelling invertebrates, including beetles, spiders and other ground-active animals. Scientists also noted that mice competed with native birds for food and altered plant and seed dynamics. In short, the mice were not merely another animal on the island. They were an introduced predator whose presence influenced much of the food web beneath the more visible birdlife.The Department of Conservation Te Papa Atawhai describes the removal operation as the Million Dollar Mouse campaign. In the winter of 2016, a 13-strong team used helicopters to spread cereal bait containing the rodent toxin brodifacoum across the main island in two applications. Monitoring followed in February 2018, when teams deployed 200 inked tracking tunnels and searched for three weeks with rodent detection dogs. No mice were detected, confirming that the eradication had succeeded.What the new research foundThe latest study examined how the island’s invertebrate communities responded in the years after mouse removal. Its headline result is striking: ground beetle abundance was reported to be roughly 40 times higher than before eradication, while rove beetle numbers had risen by more than 20 times. These are not small statistical shifts. They represent a major recovery among animals that sit close to the base of the island’s terrestrial food web.Beetles matter because they are more than a food source for birds. Ground beetles and rove beetles help process organic material, move through soil and litter layers, and form part of the predator and prey networks that keep island ecosystems functioning. When mice were present, these insects faced constant predation pressure. Once that pressure was removed, populations could rebuild across multiple breeding cycles. The new findings suggest that the recovery was not a brief rebound but a sustained ecological change.The result also fits earlier monitoring. A related study reported that invertebrate groups preyed upon by mice increased between two and 35 times after eradication, with pitfall trapping proving especially useful for ground-active animals such as beetles and spiders. The newer figures for ground and rove beetles show that some groups have continued to climb well beyond the early recovery phase.Why beetles make good messengersLarge animals often dominate conservation headlines, but invertebrates can provide some of the clearest evidence that an ecosystem is healing. They generally have short life cycles, so their populations can respond quickly when conditions improve. On Antipodes Island, this makes beetles valuable indicators of change. If mice were still suppressing insect life, the beetles would be unlikely to show such dramatic increases.Their recovery also has consequences further up the food chain. Native birds such as snipe and pipits depend on invertebrates, and earlier post-eradication surveys found that both species more than doubled after mice were removed. More insects and other invertebrates can mean more food for birds, particularly during breeding season when energy demands are high. In this way, the beetle boom is not simply a victory for beetles. It is evidence that the island’s ecological machinery is beginning to work with fewer human-caused interruptions.There is an important lesson here about patience. Conservation projects often celebrate the day a pest is declared eradicated, and understandably so. But the real measure of success may arrive years later, when native species have had time to reproduce, disperse and reclaim ecological roles. Antipodes Island shows why long-term monitoring matters. Without repeated surveys, scientists might have underestimated how deeply mouse predation had affected the island and how substantial the response could become.Recovery is not restorationThe beetle finds are encouraging, but that doesn’t mean Antipodes Island has just gone back to some pristine, original state. Ecosystems change with time, and recovery from an invasion can lead to new patterns rather than a perfect copy of the past. Some species may bounce back faster than others. Some may expand into areas they once avoided. Others may remain limited by habitat, climate or the availability of other resources.That complexity is part of what makes the study valuable. Rather than treating the island as a simple before-and-after experiment, the research helps scientists understand which parts of the ecosystem respond most strongly to predator removal. Beetles were clearly among the major beneficiaries. Their dramatic increase suggests that mice had been holding back populations for a long time, possibly preventing some species from reaching the abundance their habitat could otherwise support.It is also a reminder that eradications can have consequences beyond the target species. The Antipodes operation used a toxin that required careful planning because of possible risks to non-target wildlife. Conservation managers had to balance the damage caused by mice against the potential exposure of native birds and other animals to bait. The eventual success of the project reflects both the technical difficulty of the operation and the importance of rigorous monitoring afterwards.A signal for island conservation worldwideAntipodes Island is remote, but its story has relevance far beyond the Southern Ocean. Islands are especially vulnerable to invasive mammals because native species often evolve without defences against predators such as rodents. When mice, rats or cats arrive, they can rapidly alter food webs, prey on nesting birds and reduce invertebrate populations. Removing those invaders can therefore create unusually clear opportunities for recovery.The Antipodes results add to a growing body of evidence that pest eradication can deliver measurable ecological gains. Earlier monitoring already documented rebounds in native birds, including snipe and pipits, after mice disappeared. The beetle data now reveal recovery at a less visible but equally important level of the ecosystem. Together, these findings show that conservation action can benefit entire food webs, not only the species people most easily notice.Eight years after the mice were declared gone, the Antipodes Island has a quiet but powerful message. Sometimes the best evidence of ecological repair is not the return of the single charismatic animal but the return of the small creatures that lived in the shadows. In this case, the beetles have made themselves impossible to ignore.

articles.title: He was buried beneath a hearth, with a large stone pressed against his mouth and face, just one cm below the floor people walked on; researchers now suggest the 3,700-year-old burial was part of a magical ritual, not a punishment
articles.summary: A man buried beneath a hearth in southeastern Spain nearly 3,700 years ago may have been subjected to a ritual intended to suppress supernatural forces
articles.body: A man buried beneath a hearth in southeastern Spain nearly 3,700 years ago may have been subjected to a ritual intended to suppress supernatural forces rather than simply punish or humiliate him, according to a new archaeological study. The man’s face was positioned just one centimetre below the floor of a large hall, while a stone had been forced into his mouth and the lower part of his body lay beneath a hearth. Researchers believe the unusual arrangement may have been designed to symbolically overpower an enemy and prevent the return of forces associated with chaos.The interpretation was proposed by Marco Mazón Gomariz of the Complutense University of Madrid in a study titled 'Trampling the Enemy: A Possible Magical Ritual of Annihilation in El Argar', published in the journal 'Ilu. Revista de Ciencias de las Religiones' on October 5, 2026. The research examines the remains of an individual identified as AY5, discovered at the Bronze Age archaeological site of La Almoloya in Murcia, Spain. The author stresses that the magical-ritual explanation remains a hypothesis because the people who buried the man left no written account explaining their actions.A body hidden beneath a room's floorThe burial dates to Phase 3 of the El Argar culture, between approximately 1750 and 1550 BCE. La Almoloya was an important settlement associated with the Bronze Age society that occupied southeastern Iberia for centuries. According to the study and accompanying archaeological reports, AY5 was a man approximately 40 years old and around 1.63 metres tall. His remains were discovered in Room H9, within the settlement's first residential complex, where the body had been placed between two floor levels.The lower floor had been modified to accommodate the corpse. His lower body lay beneath a hearth, while his face was positioned at ground level, approximately one centimetre below the surface people would have walked on. A large stone had also been placed inside his mouth.The arrangement meant that people crossing the room could repeatedly step over the area covering his face. The burial contained no grave goods, unlike some other interments associated with the El Argar culture. Earlier interpretations viewed the unusual placement as a deliberate act of punishment or humiliation. The man was effectively positioned beneath the feet of people using the hall, while the stone in his mouth suggested an attempt to silence him.However, Mazón Gomariz argues that the burial may have had a more complex religious purpose.Why researchers suspect a magical ritualThe study compares AY5's burial with ancient practices in Egypt and the Near East, where the act of trampling an enemy could symbolise domination over a defeated rival. In some religious and political traditions, enemies were associated with disorder and chaos, making their symbolic destruction a way of reinforcing the power of rulers and the forces they represented. Ancient Egyptian imagery, for instance, depicted rulers trampling enemies as a demonstration of victory and the restoration of order. Similar representations appeared in the ancient Near East, where kings were shown standing over defeated opponents.The researcher also draws on evidence of magical practices intended to neutralise perceived threats. In parts of the ancient Near East, rituals against witchcraft involved figurines representing enemies or harmful forces. These objects could be damaged, buried or trampled as symbolic acts intended to defeat the threat they represented.The stone inside AY5's mouth may be significant in this context. Mazón Gomariz suggests that it could have symbolised the silencing of the individual, potentially preventing him from speaking or exerting influence even after death. The combination of the stone, the body's position beneath a hearth and the location of the face beneath a frequently used floor could therefore represent a coordinated ritual intended to keep a perceived threat under control.Was the hall more than a political space?The location of the burial also informs the new interpretation. Room H9 was a large, semi-basement hall measuring approximately 70 square metres, with benches capable of accommodating around 50 people and an elevated platform. The room also contained a sunken hearth that researchers describe as unusual for the site during this period. Its layout and access route have led scholars to examine whether the space served functions beyond ordinary domestic activities.Mazón Gomariz argues that the hall may have combined political and religious purposes. If it was used for gatherings or ceremonies, the burial's prominent position could have given the treatment of AY5 a symbolic significance for those entering or crossing the room.The man's identity, however, remains unknown. A genetic analysis has reportedly established that he was a third-degree relative of two other individuals buried at La Almoloya, suggesting that he had biological connections to the community rather than necessarily being an outsider.The researcher raises the possibility that AY5 may have held a political or religious role before losing favour, but there is no conclusive evidence identifying him as a priest, official or enemy of the settlement.An interpretation that remains unprovenThe skeleton does not show clear injuries that establish how the man died. The manner of his burial cannot, by itself, reveal whether he was killed, executed or died under other circumstances. The position of the body, the absence of grave goods and the stone in his mouth provide clues about how the living treated the dead, but they cannot definitively establish the purpose behind those actions.The study's central argument is that the burial may have been intended to suppress forces of chaos symbolically, rather than simply to humiliate a person after death. Yet, without written records from the El Argar society, the exact meaning of the ritual remains uncertain.The discovery nevertheless offers a glimpse into how Bronze Age communities may have understood death, enemies and the relationship between the physical world and supernatural threats. For now, AY5 remains an individual whose identity and fate are lost to history, while the unusual way he was buried continues to raise questions about the beliefs of the people who lived at La Almoloya.

articles.title: Meet Banu Ibrahimova, the student who designed an AI-controlled floating robot that removed up to 90.2% of a tested pollutant from model wastewater using UV light
articles.summary: Banu Ibrahimova, a student at School-Lyceum 6 in Baku, Azerbaijan, is working on a project to develop an AI-controlled floating robot that treats polluted
articles.body: Banu Ibrahimova, a student at School-Lyceum 6 in Baku, Azerbaijan, is working on a project to develop an AI-controlled floating robot that treats polluted water. The design focuses on industrial wastewater that may contain toxic cyanide-based compounds from gold mining and other industries. The project also tested the treatment method on model wastewater containing thiocyanate, phenol, and naphthalene.According to the International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF), the robot uses ultraviolet light to break down pollutants and sensors to monitor water conditions throughout the treatment process. After 42 hours of irradiation, the reported conversion efficiencies were approximately 90.2% for thiocyanate, 86.1% for phenol, and 61% for naphthalene.How UV light breaks down cyanide in industrial wastewaterThe project addresses industrial wastewater that may contain highly toxic cyanide-based compounds, including waste from gold mining and other industries. These substances can threaten ecosystems and human health. The research investigates how ultraviolet photochemical processes can transform cyanide-related species into less toxic products. Under UV light at a wavelength of 185 nanometres, water molecules split and produce highly reactive hydroxyl radicals.These radicals oxidise cyanide ions, converting them into products including ammonia and carbon dioxide. In the final step described in the pathway, nitrogen atoms can be released as nitrogen gas.UV lamps and sensors support real-time wastewater treatmentThe proposed robot is designed to float on polluted water and operate in situ. It is equipped with xenon ultraviolet lamps enclosed in quartz tubes. Modified sensors continuously monitor several conditions during treatment, including pH, temperature, conductivity, cyanide concentration, turbidity, distance, and radiation background.The project presents this arrangement as a way to monitor water during remediation. The robot is AI-controlled, and the sensor data let it assess process efficiency and optimise the photochemical cleanup in real time.How did pollutant levels change during UV treatmentThe project evaluated treatment using model wastewater containing thiocyanate, phenol, and naphthalene. Researchers monitored contaminant concentrations using ion chromatography and high-performance liquid chromatography, also known as HPLC.The reported results showed that pollutant concentrations continued to decrease as irradiation time increased. After a treatment period of 42 hours, conversion efficiencies were approximately 90.2% for thiocyanate, 86.1% for phenol, and 61% for naphthalene. The figures differ across the three substances, with thiocyanate showing the highest reported conversion efficiency and naphthalene the lowest.These results describe the performance recorded for the model wastewater under the conditions used in the project. The results show decreasing concentrations over time, with a separate conversion percentage reported for each tested contaminant during the 42-hour treatment period.A proposed approach to sustainable industrial wastewater treatmentThe project also reported intermediate products formed during treatment. Their formation was presented as confirmation that an oxidative degradation pathway had occurred. Based on the findings, the project proposes a reagent-free approach that combines photochemical treatment with real-time water monitoring.The stated aim is to provide an efficient and sustainable technology for industrial wastewater remediation. The project description does not present the method as a treatment already deployed at industrial scale; it describes the robot design and reports tests using model wastewater.
